key_figures.quote: I 2025­er­dødelighetsrisikoen­fremdeles­relativt­høysammenliknet­med­2022­og­2023­hvor­dødeligheten­varcirka­13,5 %.
key_figures.statement: The authors compare cod mortality risk in 2025 with mortality in 2022 and 2023, when it was approximately 13,5 %.

pq_notes.A1: The segment does not describe site availability or the licensing and application process. It does, however, connect disease risks with spatial planning: the authors say that IPNV can infect several farmed species, and that this cross-species transmission must be considered when planning facilities for multiple species in the same area and in coastal area planning. They also identify contact between farmed cod and wild fish at sea sites as a biosecurity concern. These are health-related considerations for siting and area planning, not a comparison of site options or a description of planning procedures.
pq_notes.A5: The authors describe research that identified leadbeaterin-1, a toxin produced by C. leadbeateri, and found it toxic to trout and salmon gill cells. A quantitative standard has been prepared, enabling measurement of toxin concentrations in seawater around fish farms during blooms; the toxin was detected in samples from the 2019 bloom and fresh water samples from 2025. The authors say monitoring could complement current methods based on algal counts, which can poorly correspond with fish deaths because the alga is small and difficult to distinguish reliably by light microscopy. Important uncertainties remain: the lethal concentrations and exposure duration are unknown, and only leadbeaterin-1 has been tested among the toxin family. The segment does not discuss spatial decision datasets or emerging siting technologies more broadly.
pq_notes.A8: The authors identify substantial biosecurity gaps in cod farming: few broodstock and juvenile facilities, contact between farmed cod and wild fish at sea sites, no marine-species-specific requirements for intake-water quality and disinfection, and no statutory screening programmes for infectious diseases. A risk map developed by the Norwegian Veterinary Institute and the Institute of Marine Research identified knowledge gaps about wild-fish susceptibility, vaccination status and non-notifiable diseases. The authors call for precautionary measures and better knowledge to improve risk assessments and reduce transmission to farmed and wild fish. They also report a cited cohabitation experiment in which IPNV from cod could infect salmon, halibut and lumpfish, making cross-species transmission relevant to multi-species facility planning and coastal area planning. Parasites may also affect both farmed and wild fish.

segments.summary:
The segment first describes harmful algal events and research on algal toxins. A 2025 bloom caused around two million fish deaths, according to the Norwegian Directorate of Fisheries. The research project ToxANoWa identified leadbeaterin-1, produced by C. leadbeateri, and showed toxicity to trout and salmon gill cells. A prepared quantitative standard makes it possible to measure the toxin in seawater; it was detected in samples from the 2019 bloom and fresh samples from 2025. The lethal concentration and exposure duration remain unknown, and algal counts may not reliably predict fish deaths. Survey respondents ranked algae as the seventh largest health problem for salmon among 38 challenges; 23 % (27 of 119) reported algal mortality and 24 % perceived occurrence as increasing.

The main chapter reviews farmed cod health and welfare. Cod production increased: 8,7 million fish were stocked and approximately 19 700 tonnes slaughtered in 2025. Mortality risk in the grow-out phase was 20,4 %, down from 22,2 % in 2024. Problems include intestinal disease, poor-performing fish, skeletal and jaw deformities, and maturation-related welfare concerns. Gill disease and vibriosis appear to have become more important. The segment reports 33 serious welfare incidents and describes findings from 25 Veterinary Institute submissions from eight sites. It also outlines infection risks, including transmission between farmed cod and wild fish, and IPNV transmission among farmed species. The authors identify major biosecurity knowledge and regulatory gaps and recommend precautionary measures. Evidence includes official data, institute submissions, cited research and a survey of fish-health personnel; several causal relationships and disease risks remain uncertain.

key_figures.statement: The authors report that over 19 million cleaner fish were deployed in the preceding year and 12,8 million were recorded dead.

key_figures.quote: Oppdrettere innrapporterte 75 alvorlige velferdsmessige hendelser for rensefisk i sjø til Mattilsynet i 2025.

key_figures.quote: For rognkjeks svarte fem av 33 respondenter at de registrerte god effekt, en liten økning fra 2024, mens syv respondenter mente at de så liten eller ingen effekt.
key_figures.statement: In the 2025 survey, five of 33 respondents reported good cleaner-louse-eating effect for lumpfish, while seven reported little or no effect.

pq_notes.A5: This segment concerns fish health rather than spatial decision-making or emerging technology, so it provides no direct evidence about the knowledge base or technologies used for spatial decisions. It does report that in 2025 a first international report of Piscirickettsia salmonis in turbot was confirmed using immunohistochemistry and in situ hybridisation after culture failed. The outbreak followed suboptimal water quality and was controlled by improving environmental conditions. Cleaner-fish mortality data are described as difficult to interpret because of incomplete accounting and undocumented losses; a new reporting form was introduced from 01.01.2026 to improve data on health, welfare and mortality.
pq_notes.A7: The segment offers fish-health management observations rather than guidance on efficient spatial use. Survey respondents emphasized suitable tank design, size grading to reduce aggression and injuries, sorting by fin condition, appropriate species-specific feed, and gentle handling. In sea cages they highlighted planning and follow-up, adequate shelter and feed, and gentle handling during delousing and net cleaning. The report says cleaner fish tolerate crowding, netting and pumping less well than salmon, and welfare remains poor with high mortality. Respondents also reported that discontinuing cleaner-fish use sometimes increased lice pressure and delousing, while others described positive outcomes. The authors conclude that cleaner-fish use should be phased out or stopped if welfare cannot be improved; the Veterinary Institute has previously proposed ending use by 2029 at the latest.
pq_notes.A8: The authors describe disease transmission risks where cleaner fish and salmon share cages. Wild-caught cleaner fish have unknown infection status and can carry agents including atypical Aeromonas salmonicida; introduction from other regions may also create biosecurity risks. Experimental evidence shows Paramoeba perurans can pass between cleaner fish and farmed fish, and a 2022 site detection of Spironucleus salmonicida in both salmon and lumpfish suggests possible cross-species transmission. Lumpfish are vulnerable to infection from salmon with S. salmonicida and are considered unsuitable as cleaner fish at sites with outbreaks. The report also notes potential transmission of other agents and emphasizes monitoring infection dynamics, particularly for pathogens with marine reservoirs.

segments.summary:
This segment opens Chapter 13 on health in farmed marine species and then includes a substantial portion of Chapter 14 on cleaner-fish health and welfare. It describes limited Norwegian production of halibut, turbot and spotted wolffish, their biological and production characteristics, and reported bacterial, viral and parasitic diseases. Halibut production remained between 2 and 7000 tonnes in 2020–2024. In 2025, Piscirickettsia salmonis was detected in turbot for the first time internationally, at a site where increased mortality followed suboptimal water quality; improving environmental conditions controlled the outbreak. The Veterinary Institute received 19 submissions from three sites, six from turbot and 13 from halibut, and none from spotted wolffish.

The cleaner-fish discussion reports continued contraction in use: more than 19 million were deployed in 2025, 69 % below the 2019 peak, and reporting sites declined from 444 in 2019 to 148 in 2025. The text describes welfare concerns, disease risks from wild-caught fish, and practical challenges including unsuitable cage conditions, handling, feeding and mortality measurement. A new reporting form began 01.01.2026. Survey evidence indicates uncertainty about cleaner fish’s lice-control effect, while disease transmission between cleaner fish and salmon remains a biosecurity concern. The segment draws on official records, diagnostic submissions, literature and respondent surveys; it notes limitations including incomplete mortality records, uncertain pathogen significance and small or non-representative survey samples.

pq_notes.A8: This segment reports survey respondents' perceptions of health problems in farmed fish, including problems that they associated with mortality, reduced welfare or increasing occurrence. It does not discuss biosecurity, disease transmission between farms, water connectivity, or how those factors affect siting and operations.

segments.summary: This segment contains appendices presenting survey results on perceived health problems in farmed fish. It covers salmon in grow-out facilities, including results by grouped production areas; rainbow trout and cod in grow-out facilities; salmon broodstock; lumpfish and cleaner fish in hatcheries; and lumpfish and cleaner fish co-reared with salmon. Fish-health personnel and inspectors or advisers from the Norwegian Food Safety Authority were asked to identify important problems from specified lists, judging whether they contributed to mortality, reduced growth, reduced welfare or increasing occurrence. The number of respondents differs by species, production setting and question category. For example, the salmon grow-out survey had N=119 respondents for mortality and reduced welfare, while the regional salmon breakdown groups respondents into PO1-PO5 (N=41), PO6-9 (N=39) and PO10-13 (N=26). The appendices also define abbreviations for health conditions shown in the figures. A final acknowledgement states that 143 professionals answered the survey and thanks data providers, producers and other contributors. The evidence presented is based on reported professional perceptions, not a direct measurement of disease incidence or causal effects. The figures are reproduced as charts, and this segment does not explain spatial planning, aquaculture siting, environmental assessment, competing coastal uses or regulatory processes.
